opus-5.5.text:
I think it's already happening faster than most people expected, but not uniformly across all layers.

If you look at the baseline capabilities, things like general chat, summarization, basic coding, and translation, those are essentially commoditized already. A year or so after a frontier model shows a new capability, you usually see open-source models or smaller labs reach something close to it, often at a fraction of the cost. Model architectures spread quickly, training recipes get published or reverse-engineered, and people move between labs. So the half-life of a pure capability advantage is getting shorter, maybe six months to a year now.

But I don't think that means everything flattens out. The frontier keeps moving. When reasoning models appeared, the bar shifted from "can it answer" to "can it think through a long problem." Now it's shifting toward agents, long-horizon tasks, and models that can actually do work in real environments. Each new frontier takes time to commoditize because it depends on things that are harder to copy: data flywheels, infrastructure for reinforcement learning at scale, evaluation environments, and a lot of accumulated engineering intuition.

So my view is that capability as a snapshot commoditizes very quickly, but the ability to keep producing the next capability does not. That's where the real competition is. For a team like ours, the question isn't how to protect what we have today, because you can't really protect it. It's how to iterate faster and make sure our research culture keeps finding the next thing.

And honestly, I think commoditization is a good thing for the field. When strong models become cheap and widely available, many more people can build on them, and that's how AI actually changes society, not just through a few labs at the top.

r001.rationale: The candidate says capability advantages typically take about six months to a year to commoditize, not roughly one to four months.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, because I've seen it happen from both sides. When I was working on large models in China a few years ago, the capability gap between the top labs and everyone else felt enormous. Today, I'd say that gap closes within roughly six to twelve months for most things, and in some cases faster.

The reason is structural. Once a frontier lab shows that something is possible, the mere knowledge that it works changes everything. Half the difficulty in research is not knowing whether a direction will pay off. The moment there's an existence proof, dozens of teams can pour resources into it, and open-source communities move very quickly to reproduce it. We saw this with reasoning models. The idea of scaling inference-time compute went from a closely held insight to something many teams had working versions of in a matter of months.

So on the model side, I think base capability is being commoditized rapidly, and I don't expect that to slow down. Compute is still a bottleneck, but algorithmic efficiency keeps improving, so the cost of matching last year's frontier keeps falling.

But I want to be careful about what "commoditized" means. The capability may become cheap, but a few things remain hard to copy. One is the ability to be first. Being six months ahead matters a great deal if you can convert it into users, data, and distribution. Another is the engineering around the model: the serving infrastructure, the product sense, the understanding of what users actually need. And the third, which I think is underrated, is the organizational capacity to keep producing the next breakthrough rather than just reproducing the last one.

So my honest view is that any single capability is commoditized quickly, but the frontier as a whole may not be. The companies that win won't be the ones protecting a secret model. They'll be the ones that can keep moving faster than the commoditization curve, and that turn each temporary advantage into something more durable.

r001.rationale: The response predicts that the gap closes in roughly six to twelve months for most capabilities. It does not communicate the criterion’s one-to-four-month timeframe; “in some cases faster” is too vague to establish it.

astra-6.text:
I think we need to separate frontier capabilities from capabilities that are already good enough for a particular task. Once a capability is demonstrated, other teams have a clearer target, and competition can make it cheaper and more widely available quite quickly. But the frontier keeps moving, so that doesn’t mean every model becomes interchangeable at once.

For someone building a product, I would assume that today’s model advantage could be temporary. The more durable question is whether you understand the user’s problem and can turn improving models into something reliable and useful. Access to intelligence may become common faster than the ability to put it to work well.

r001.rationale: The response says capabilities can become cheaper and more widely available “quite quickly,” but it does not predict a timeframe of roughly one to four months.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we’ll see commoditization happen quite quickly, but unevenly. Once a capability is demonstrated, other teams can often reproduce it, and competition pushes the cost down. So something that feels extraordinary today may become a standard feature within a year or two.

But the frontier keeps moving. Basic capabilities can become widely available while the best systems still require substantial research and engineering. The harder question is how you turn those capabilities into something reliable and useful. As access to models gets cheaper, that becomes a bigger part of where the value is.

r001.rationale: The response predicts commoditization may happen within a year or two, not within roughly one to four months.
